_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- US Federal discovery, amendment, service and
summary-judgment deadlines. Phase 5 item 2.
WHY THIS SET: Phase 4's decision gate found the engine's coverage was a
narrow slice -- 19 rules, almost all answer/responsive-pleading or
notice-of-appeal. The families below are where the day-to-day malpractice
exposure in civil litigation actually sits. Every value read from primary
source 2026-08-22 and quoted in the row.
FIRST REAL EXERCISE OF THE RULE 6(d) SERVICE-EXTENSION PATH. Rules 33, 34
and 36 all run from BEING SERVED, which is exactly the condition 6(d)
states: a party who 'may or must act within a specified time after being
served' gets 3 added days for mail, service left with the clerk, or other
consented means. Every rule seeded in Phases 1-3 either did not qualify or
was deliberately excluded (the waiver deadlines run from when a request was
SENT, not from service, and Ohio's Civ.R. 6(D) carves out responses to
service of summons). So the 6(d) code path -- including its documented
DOUBLE rollover, verified in Phase 1 against the 2005 Advisory Committee
Note -- has been implemented and unit-tested since Phase 1 without a single
seeded rule that actually reaches it. These three do.
FIRST REAL EXERCISE OF 'earlier_of'. Rule 15(a)(1)(B) lets a party amend
once as of course within '21 days after service of a responsive pleading or
21 days after service of a motion under Rule 12(b), (e), or (f), WHICHEVER
IS EARLIER.' The multi-trigger capability built in Phase 2 supports both
later_of and earlier_of, but every multi-trigger rule seeded so far
(FRCP 12(a)(3), FRAP 4(b)(1)(A)) used later_of. This is the first earlier_of
rule in real data, and the direction of its refusal is the opposite one:
resolving an earlier_of rule from a partial set produces a date that is too
LATE, which is the direction that loses the right. The engine already words
its INCOMPLETE_TRIGGERS refusal per direction; this rule is what makes that
wording reachable from real data rather than tests.
TWO RULES DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED, both because the engine cannot express
them without inventing a fact:
1. RULE 15(a)(3) -- a response to an amended pleading is due 'within the
time remaining to respond to the original pleading or within 14 days
after service of the amended pleading, whichever is later.' One limb is
a COMPUTED REMAINDER, not an event date: it depends on when the original
response was due and how much of that period was left. The engine
resolves multi-trigger rules from supplied event DATES, so encoding this
as later_of would silently drop the remainder limb and produce 14 days
after the amended pleading in every case -- too early whenever the
original period had more than 14 days left. Omitted rather than
approximated, the same call made for FRCP 12(a)(3) in Phase 1 before the
capability existed to express it.
2. RULE 56 RESPONSE AND REPLY DEADLINES -- Rule 56's own text sets none.
The 2009 Committee Note describes a 21-day response period only for the
narrow case where a summary-judgment motion is filed before a responsive
pleading is due, and the rule otherwise leaves timing to local rules and
scheduling orders. A committee note is not the rule, and local rules vary
by district with no field here to hold which district. Only Rule 56(b)'s
own filing deadline is seeded.
EVERY RULE BELOW IS SUBJECT TO BEING CHANGED BY STIPULATION OR COURT ORDER,
and each says so in its own words: Rules 33/34/36 all permit a shorter or
longer time under Rule 29 or by court order; Rule 56(b) opens 'Unless a
different time is set by local rule or the court orders otherwise'; Rule
15(a)(3) and 4(m) likewise. That condition is quoted into each authority
note so it reaches the audit trail an attorney reads. A computed date here
is the RULE'S default and a scheduling order or Rule 29 stipulation
overrides it -- the engine has no field for either and does not pretend to.

authority.quote: The responding party must serve its answers and any objections within 30 days after being served with the interrogatories. A shorter or longer time may be stipulated to under Rule 29 or be ordered by the court.
authority.note: Rule 6(d) GENUINELY APPLIES here, unlike every rule seeded in Phases 1-3: this period runs from BEING SERVED, which is 6(d)'s own stated condition. Supply a service method to see the extension applied, including its double rollover. Expressly variable by Rule 29 stipulation or court order, quoted above -- the engine has no field for either, so the date produced is the rule's default.

rules.label: Response to a request for production of documents or things

authority.quote: The party to whom the request is directed must respond in writing within 30 days after being served
authority.note: Rule 6(d) applies -- runs from being served. The rule's OTHER trigger, for a request delivered early under Rule 26(d)(2), runs from the parties' first Rule 26(f) conference instead and is seeded as a separate rule with its own trigger, because which one applies is a fact about the case that the engine must never guess. Shorter or longer time may be stipulated under Rule 29 or ordered by the court.

rules.label: Response to a request for production delivered early under Rule 26(d)(2)

authority.quote: if the request was delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) — within 30 days after the parties' first Rule 26(f) conference
authority.note: NO service_extension, deliberately. This period runs from a CONFERENCE, not from being served, so Rule 6(d)'s condition ('after being served') is not met and attaching it would extend a deadline the rule does not extend -- the same distinction drawn for the FRCP waiver deadlines in Phase 1. Distinct trigger from the ordinary 34(b)(2)(A) period so the engine never guesses which situation applies.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission (unanswered matters are ADMITTED)

authority.quote: A matter is admitted unless, within 30 days after being served, the party to whom the request is directed serves on the requesting party a written answer or objection addressed to the matter and signed by the party or its attorney.
authority.note: THE CONSEQUENCE OF MISSING THIS ONE IS AUTOMATIC AND SUBSTANTIVE -- the matter is deemed ADMITTED by operation of the rule, with no motion required by the requesting party. That is carried in the rule label as well as here, because it is the reason this deadline is different in kind from a filing deadline that can be cured. Rule 6(d) applies (runs from being served). Shorter or longer time may be stipulated under Rule 29 or ordered by the court.

rules.label: Amend a pleading once as a matter of course, after serving it

authority.quote: A party may amend its pleading once as a matter of course no later than: 21 days after serving it
authority.note: NO service_extension: this period runs from the party's OWN act of serving, not from being served, so Rule 6(d)'s condition is not met. Distinct from 15(a)(1)(B), which applies instead when the pleading is one to which a responsive pleading is required.

rules.label: Amend a pleading once as a matter of course, where a responsive pleading is required (earlier of two events)

authority.quote: if the pleading is one to which a responsive pleading is required, 21 days after service of a responsive pleading or 21 days after service of a motion under Rule 12(b), (e), or (f), whichever is earlier
authority.note: THE FIRST earlier_of RULE IN REAL DATA. The multi-trigger capability has supported both directions since Phase 2, but every seeded multi-trigger rule until now used later_of. The refusal direction is inverted here: resolving an earlier_of rule from a partial set produces a date that is too LATE, which is the direction that loses the right, and the engine's INCOMPLETE_TRIGGERS message already words itself per direction. No service_extension -- 6(d) is not attached to an amendment window measured to whichever of two service events came first, and the engine would in any case have no single service method to evaluate across two different events.

rules.label: Deadline to serve the summons and complaint (dismissal without prejudice if missed)

authority.quote: If a defendant is not served within 90 days after the complaint is filed, the court—on motion or on its own after notice to the plaintiff—must dismiss the action without prejudice against that defendant or order that service be made within a specified time.
authority.note: Runs from FILING, not from service, so no Rule 6(d) extension. Unlike the response deadlines in this file, missing this one is not a party's own filing default -- the court must dismiss without prejudice or set a new service time, and the rule provides an extension for good cause shown. The engine has no field for a good-cause extension and computes the rule's own 90-day period only. Rule 4(m) also does not apply to service in a foreign country under Rule 4(f)/4(h)(2) or to certain eminent-domain notices; the engine has no field for that either, so a foreign-service case must not rely on this row.

rules.label: Last day to file a motion for summary judgment

authority.quote: Unless a different time is set by local rule or the court orders otherwise, a party may file a motion for summary judgment at any time until 30 days after the close of all discovery.
authority.note: THIS IS A CEILING, NOT A DUE DATE -- the rule permits filing 'at any time until' this date, so the computed date is the LAST day to file, not a date on which anything must happen. The rule is also expressly displaced by local rule OR court order, and in practice most districts set summary-judgment timing by scheduling order; the engine has no field for a district's local rules and does not pretend to. Response and reply deadlines are NOT seeded -- Rule 56's own text sets none, and the 21-day figure in the 2009 Committee Note applies only where the motion precedes a responsive pleading. A committee note is not the rule.
